demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette: Mateo Vance was thirty-two when the Oakridge High science wing became a room he could no longer enter without his breath shortening. He had been conducting a safety walkthrough during third period, his back turned to assist a student with a worksheet in the adjacent study carrel. When he turned back, a heavy glass reagent bottle had tipped, spreading a corrosive liquid across the tile as a sophomore lunged backward and caught his forearm on a jagged edge of shattered glass. The boy's immediate cry was followed by the sharp, chemical tang that filled the hallway. By the time Mateo dropped to his knees, pressing sterile gauze against the wound, the damage was already done. The sight of blood mixing with the cleaning solution, the boy's wide, stunned eyes, and the clinical scent of the triage room where he was taken would not leave him. In the months that followed, Mateo found himself unable to sit quietly. He kept his mind perpetually occupied with departmental reports, email chains, and lesson plans. He deliberately avoided speaking with the school resource officer who had come to the building, steering clear of any uniformed personnel entirely. When thoughts of the lab forced their way in, he pushed them aside, yet they returned without context or sequence. He knew exactly what had happened, but he could never find the words to describe it. The memory arrived as if it were unfolding in the present tense. The heat of the fluorescent lights, the slickness on the linoleum, the sharp sting of antiseptic, and the boy's choked gasp pressed against him simultaneously. Alongside this full sensory reliving came a racing heart, trembling hands, and a constant tightening in his throat. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by that single misstep. He could no longer trust that he would act correctly in any moment requiring quick judgment. Self-blame settled heavily on his chest each evening. Alongside it came waves of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. Sleep became impossible. He stopped lying down after midnight, choosing instead to remain awake in the armchair in his office, certain that staying alert was the only way to prevent another disaster. Stress in his daily routine, particularly during administrative reviews, now routinely triggered the same physical reactivity he had tried to outrun. When his wife asked about his exhaustion, he would deflect with technical details about curriculum compliance, though his jaw tightened and his breathing grew shallow whenever the conversation neared school safety protocols. The avoidance formed a quiet routine. He stopped volunteering for field trips and requested a transfer away from the science wing, a change that left him quietly isolated in the counseling office. Colleagues noticed he flinched at the smell of industrial cleaner during custodial rounds or at the sharp, medicinal odor of the school nurse's antiseptic wipes. A recent annual physical brought another layer of tension. Lying on the examination table, waiting for the doctor's stethoscope to press against his chest, Mateo's heart rate spiked and his vision tunneled. He had come to believe that medical procedures were inescapable reminders of the clinic where the boy was taken, and the sensation of the cold metal against his skin left him unable to speak. What frightened him most was that the memory would not stay in the past, that his own hands felt unreliable, that his marriage and his career were fracturing under the weight of what he could not explain. It was the cumulative presence of these unspoken moments, the fact that he could no longer walk past the gymnasium without his breath catching, that finally brought him to intake. He sat across from the clinician now, hands clasped tightly, not sure how to begin. What he most hoped for was to reclaim the ability to focus on a student's needs without his mind fracturing into the past. What he feared most was that the guilt would never stop dictating his next move.
